definition: Innocuous means harmless and inoffensive — unable to injure anyone or to ruffle anyone's feelings.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word innocuous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know innocuous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The question sounded innocuous — 'Where did you grow up?' — but the diplomat had learned that no question at that table ever was.
Mild stops short of innocuous: a mild remark still carries a trace of sting, while an innocuous one has none to carry at all.
Anodyne goes further than innocuous — the innocuous merely does no harm, while the anodyne has been scrubbed so clean of edge that it no longer says much of anything.

Harmless is the plain, physical word: it does no damage — a harmless spider, a harmless dose. Innocuous reaches further, promising that the thing will neither injure anyone nor even ruffle anyone; it covers feelings as well as bodies.
Inoffensive means giving no offense — nobody's feelings are bruised. Innocuous makes the larger claim: no offense and no injury of any kind, which is why lab reports and security sweeps reach for it.

Innocuous means harmless and inoffensive — unable to injure anyone or to ruffle anyone's feelings.
The 'suspicious device' that emptied the terminal for an hour proved entirely innocuous: a child's science-fair project, a shoebox of wires and glitter built to measure humidity.
Notice where the word does its work: harm was expected, searched for, and found absent.
Innocuous covers both fronts at once — the shoebox can neither injure anyone nor offend anyone — and it appears most often exactly here, at the moment a feared thing is cleared.
neutral / faintly dismissive
Innocuous most often appears where harm was suspected — a 'seemingly innocuous' email, a package that proves innocuous — so the word carries a small sigh of relief.
Applied to art or conversation it turns faintly dismissive: an innocuous little comedy is safe and forgettable.
Its dark twin noxious (met in the root check above) is the same root with the harm left in.

The hum began in November, a low pulse in the walls of the new apartment block that residents could feel in their teeth.
Theories multiplied: a gas leak, failing wiring, something wrong with the water mains.
One tenant kept a packed suitcase by the door.
The city sent an inspector, who spent two days with a stethoscope against the walls and a vibration gauge in the stairwells.

Her report was almost disappointing: the source was a ventilation fan with a worn bearing, and the vibration was innocuous — it could not spark, leak, weaken a beam, or do anything at all beyond being heard.
The fan was oiled on a Tuesday.
By December, several residents admitted they missed having something to talk about.
